body.text: The CLI writes it one time (new app). Then it is yours.

children.title: Today

body.text: dotnet builds it. It selects the SDK and adds the host packages and the engine package, each with a version.

items.label: Without it
items.value: Nothing builds. It selects the SDK and the packages.

body.text: CLI: new app writes it, init adds the SDK and the engine package, update sets the versions. Engine: checks each Umpire version (UMP030201).

body.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <Sdk Name="Umpire.Sdk" />
  <PropertyGroup>
    <RootNamespace>Shop</RootNamespace>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Umpire.Vsa.Hosts.Web" Version="0.2.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Umpire.Vsa.Views" Version="0.2.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Umpire.Engine.Build" Version="0.2.0"
                      PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: Managed, one line

body.text: A web SDK variant brings the web host packages and the engine package with its own version. The root namespace is the project name by default.

Nothing to edit by hand

items.title: Lose

items.title: global.json
items.summary: .NET SDK version, Umpire.Sdk version, test runner

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: dotnet reads it before all phases. The Umpire.Sdk entry is required: an SDK in a Sdk attribute gets its version only from here. The .NET SDK pin is for stability.

items.label: Without it
items.value: Sdk="Umpire.Sdk" has no version, so the build stops. The test runner falls back to VSTest.

body.text: CLI: init writes it, update sets the pin, and the CLI finds the app folder from it. Engine: reads the pin for UMP030201.

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: No change

body.text: dotnet needs it before the build, and it is the one Umpire version place. The CLI calls its folder the "app folder", so it does not clash with the block folder of the engine.

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: NuGet reads it in restore. It adds the umpire feed with a GITHUB_TOKEN, because GitHub Packages needs a sign-in, also for public packages.

items.label: Without it
items.value: Restore fails: the Umpire packages are only on GitHub Packages.

body.text: CLI: init writes it, or adds the feed to your file.

body.code:
<packageSources>
  <clear />
  <add key="umpire" value="https://nuget.pkg.github.com/MgCohen/index.json" />
  <add key="nuget.org" value="https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json" />
</packageSources>
<packageSourceCredentials>
  <umpire>
    <add key="Username" value="umpire" />
    <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%GITHUB_TOKEN%" />
  </umpire>
</packageSourceCredentials>

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: Remove, after nuget.org

body.text: Publish the stable versions to nuget.org. NuGet reads nuget.org by default, so the app needs no feed file and no token.

items.title: Lose

items.title: Directory.Build.props
items.summary: Only the build output in artifacts~

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: MSBuild reads it before the SDK props. It sends the build output to artifacts~. Unity skips each folder that ends with ~, so a Unity project does not import the DLLs a second time.

items.label: Without it
items.value: bin/ and obj/ are next to the code. The build still works.

body.text: CLI: init adds the 2 properties (build-output step). No tool of ours reads it.

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: Remove, the SDK does it

body.text: Umpire.Sdk sets the 2 properties before it imports the .NET SDK, so the same output layout needs no file. A web app needs Umpire.Sdk.Web, because the web SDK imports the .NET SDK first.

children.title: Trade-offs
children.summary: What we win, lose and change

items.title: Win
items: One file less
One init step less

items.title: Lose
items: Nothing, if the proof passes

items.title: Change
items: Needs Umpire.Sdk.Web (same as Shop.csproj)
A proof: the web host and a nested test project write to one artifacts~

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: It pins one version of the umpire tool for this app, so dotnet umpire runs the same version as the packages. It is a stability pin, not behavior: the build and the check do not read it.

items.label: Without it
items.value: dotnet umpire does not run. The build and the check still work.

body.text: CLI: init writes it, update sets the version. Engine: compares the tool version with the packages (UMP030201).

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: Remove; the pin moves to global.json

body.text: The app keeps no tool file. You install the tool one time for your machine, not for each app. The stability check stays: at each start, the CLI compares its version with the Umpire.Sdk pin in global.json.

body.code:
dotnet tool install -g Umpire.Cli
umpire add module Orders

items.title: .editorconfig
items.summary: The native .NET rules of the IDE and the compiler

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: .NET owns this file. The IDE and the compiler read it. Our docs also tell you to put the Umpire rule values here, so Umpire keys are mixed with the native rules.

items.label: Without it
items.value: The native rules use the .NET defaults and the Umpire.Sdk settings.

body.text: Not ours.

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: No change to the file

body.text: We never write it and never move it. It keeps only native rules, and you change a native rule here as in each .NET project. The Umpire keys go to the definition (see umpire.rules.globalconfig). Later, the engine can read the native results into its report.

children.title: Trade-offs
children.summary: What we win, lose and change

items.title: Win
items: The native IDE flow stays as it is
No Umpire keys in a .NET file

items.title: Lose
items: Nothing

items.title: Change

items.title: umpire.rules.globalconfig
items.summary: The Umpire rule values of this app

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: The file does not exist. The Umpire values are in the analyzer packages, and you change them in .editorconfig.

items.label: Without it
items.value: The Umpire analyzers use the pack defaults.

body.text: Not ours today: hand-written keys in a native file.

children.title: Proposal
children.summary: New, generated

body.text: You write the Umpire values in the definition. The engine writes this file in the block, and you commit it. Umpire.Sdk gives it to the compiler. The IDE runs the Umpire analyzers with it. The API below is a sketch.

body.code:
# Generated by the Umpire engine from ShopArchitecture. Do not edit.
is_global = true
umpire.UMP010101.max = 140
dotnet_diagnostic.UMP010203.severity = warning

children.title: Today
children.summary: What it does, who owns it, what breaks without it

body.text: It changes the result of the check. Each line is one error that you accept for now. The engine removes the accepted errors from the report, so the build passes, but each new error fails it. Thus an existing app can adopt Umpire and fix its old errors one at a time.

items.label: Without it
items.value: Each existing error fails the build, so an old app cannot start with Umpire.

body.text: Engine: writes it on request, reads it in each check (Baseline step).

body.cap: Write the baseline from the errors of this build

body.text: It is not on Umpire.Sdk. It repeats the build settings of the SDK and pins the NUnit versions.

items.label: Without it
items.value: No unit tests and no architecture tests.

body.text: CLI: new app writes it. Engine: checks the Umpire versions.

body.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <EnableNUnitRunner>true</EnableNUnitRunner>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="../Shop.csproj" />
    <PackageReference Include="Umpire.Vsa.Testing.Unit" Version="0.2.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="NUnit" Version="4.6.1" />
    <PackageReference Include="NUnit3TestAdapter" Version="6.3.1" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
